slidelink.displaytext: CEO Spoof: Don't Take the Bait
How to Spot a CEO Spoof Four warning signs:

slidetranscripts.slidetranscript:
<Document xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xmlns:xsd="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"> <Content> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Last quarter, GitHub ran an internal phishing simulation.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="38 percent of employees clicked a link in a CEO spoof email.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="The most common reason employees gave: it looked urgent, and it came from the top.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="This type of attack is called a CEO spoof. And it works, because we are wired to respond quickly to authority. This short module will help you slow down and spot the signs." /> </Block> </Content> </Document>

<Document xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xmlns:xsd="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"> <Content> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="CEO spoof emails share a set of recognizable patterns. Here are four signs to watch for.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="First: the sender address doesn't match the official domain. One changed character is enough to fool a quick glance.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Second: the message creates urgency without giving details. Vague requests like "I need a favor" or "handle this today" are designed to make you act before you think.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Third: you are asked to open an attachment, click a link, share credentials, or transfer funds. These are the actual goals of the attack, but they often only appear after you respond to the first message.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Fourth: the email blocks your ability to verify. "I'm in meetings, can't call" keeps you in a channel the attacker controls. This is how two-stage attacks work: the first message is harmless. The real request comes once you reply.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="If you spot any of these signs, stop. Don't reply, don't open anything. Reach out to the sender directly through a different channel." /> </Block> </Content> </Document>

<Document xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xmlns:xsd="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"> <Content> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Now let's apply what you have just learned.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Below you will see an email that was flagged during our simulation. Take a moment to read it, then click on every element that looks suspicious to you." /> </Block> </Content> </Document>

<Document xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xmlns:xsd="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"> <Content> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="You're ready. Here is what to do when you receive a suspicious email.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="First: do not reply, click, or open any attachments.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Second: verify through a different channel. Ask a colleague, reach out via Slack, or call the sender directly.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Third: report the email. Select it and use Report, then Phishing. This helps protect everyone." /> </Block> </Content> </Document>
